Mr. Chairman, we think we can move through this stage quite quickly. The Opposition has one main concern with respect to Bill C-150, and that is simply: Do we have it right this time? The Assembly of First Nations has looked at it and my office has looked at it and we think we do. However, we were fooled before. Therefore, we are seeking your guidance, Mr. Chairman. My hon. friend and colleague from the New Democratic Party has consulted with the Law and Government Division in the Research Branch of the Library of Parliament and we think that if there were a small improvement made to the accompanying note, we might both then be satisfied.
I will not try to intrude on his territory in this respect because he has done the background work, but I would like your advice, Mr. Chairman. Can we now, under Clause 1, make a modest clarifying amendment to the accompanying note. If so, I will yield to my hon. friend to make the appropriate motion.
Subject to whether or not the motion is in order, most certainly the Member can proceed to introduce that amendment at the present time.

The difficulty there has been is well known across the country. The Bill, as it was originally drafted, under Clauses 6 and 11, inhibited certain people whose parents died prior to April 17, 1985, and another case is in relation to entitlement from 1987. The intention of the amendment which has been drafted by a legal counsel to our committee, Bruce Carson, has been shown to the Minister and to my hon. friend from Cochrane-Superior. I believe it is in order and acceptable to the Government and to the two opposition Parties.

This amendment, which adds the underlined words, would modify the rules respecting entitlement of persons to registration so that the date of death of a parent or other ancestor would not be a factor in determining such entitlement.
To ensure that we do not run into the problem with justice or departmental interpretation, as we have found over the past more than a year, which affected many women and their children, we would add these words following the word "entitlement":
-as it is not the purpose of this Act to erect barriers to entitlement to registration.
That simply adds clarification in terms of departmental officials and others interpreting what our intentions are in adding the words "(f) or subsection (2)" and "provision". It will make it abundantly clear, for interpretation, that it was not the intention of Parliament previously to bring in a death rule and that it is certainly not the intention of Parliament now, nor of any of the Parties in this House, to prolong or carry on with the death rule. Therefore, I would so move, and I
believe my friend from Cochrane-Superior would second this amendment. The Minister has a copy, as does my friend.

As I understand it, the Table Officers will be checking the amendment to see that it is in order. However, they do advise me that if this is an amendment to the explanatory notes as opposed to the Bill, it will create some problems.

Mr. Chairman, I understand the approach. There is always some problem. There is always something in the way, some reason that one cannot do something. We get so weary of living with that.
However, there is a way in Parliament in which we can get around that. That is simply if you, Mr. Chairman, will seek unanimous consent to proceed to modify the explanatory note as suggested by my hon. friend, we could then proceed with dispatch. We do not need to search, then, through Beauchesne's and all manner of precedents. I think that we can do this, provided that the Government is willing and there is no Member of Parliament who objects. I think in this way we can proceed expeditiously.

I do want to hear from the Minister. Perhaps, just before he comments, I can say that my advice is that what we are doing and what Parliament always does is adopt the various clauses of the Bill and adopt the Bill itself but not adopt the explanatory notes. Therefore perhaps counsel can make some modifications in them, but this House does not adopt the explanatory notes themselves. With that, perhaps the Minister has some comment.

Hon. Bernard Valcourt, Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development) moved, for the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, that the Bill be read the third time and do pass.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today, and my comments will be brief, to ask the House to consider and provide quick passage of Bill C-150, an Act to amend the Indian Act. It is understood that with the consent of the two Opposition Parties, we shall proceed with all stages of Bill today.
This Bill will eliminate from the present Act a number of provisions that would otherwise unfairly deprive certain persons of their entitlement to registration as Indians.
The proposed amendments are directly connected with major progressive changes introcuced by this Government in 1985 with respect to the Indian Act, changes that were subsequently adopted by Parliament. These changes, known as Bill C-31, were aimed at bringing the provisions of the Indian Act into line with the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, by eliminating discriminatory provisions, restoring Indian status and band membership and increasing control of Indians over their own affairs.
As a result, we have ensured that men and women receive equal treatment, that children are treated fairly, whether or not they were born out of wedlock, that people who lost their Indian status as a result of discriminatory measures or enfranchisement could recover their status, and finally, that the direct descendants of such persons would also have registration entitlement.
Indian Act

Bill C-31 was a major step forward in the history and progress of Canada's Indian people. The response to the opportunities afforded by these amendments has been heavy.
To date, more than 45,000 Indians have been registered under the new provisions, and applications are still being received at the rate of some 35 per day. In the initial stages, some backlog in processing applications occurred, but this backlog is now being eliminated.
The Government, of course, is committed to provide additional funding to Indian bands as a consequence of the increase in membership and the social and other needs these increases engender. The commitment has been met, although some say partially. Funding for the implementation of Bill C-31 has nearly doubled in the past 12 months, from $40 million in 1987-88 to some $72 million in the current year.
In general, the provisions of Bill C-31 are working well and have been well received by native Canadians.

However, although this Bill was carefully drafted, after thorough consultation with the groups concerned, the Government was advised that a provision of the present Act might have the effect of excluding certain persons we had no intention of excluding.
This technical error arises basically from the so-called "death rule" which adversely affects requests for registration based on the initial right of the person's granparents. More specifically, it affects applicants if one or both parents were deceades before April 17, 1985. This was clearly a mistake, and we acted as quickly as possible to draft the requisite amendment.
In the process, we received the positive and unanimous support of the Assembly of First Nations, the Native Council of Canada, the Native Women's Association and other native groups.
Members of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs, on both sides of the House, also agreed this matter should be dealt with as soon as possible.
The changes proposed today will correct the situation.
They have been made retroactive to April 17, 1985, to ensure justice and fairness, not only to future applicants but to those whose applications are now before us.
The total number of individuals directly affected by this measure is relatively small. However, that is not the main point. The entire purpose behind Bill C-31 was to eliminate discrimination and ensure fairness in the Indian Act. Even if only one person was unjustly denied status, it would be one too many. It is for that reason that I urge all Members in all

Parties, and we have their co-operation, to give speedy passage to the Bill in order that it may be enacted into law at the earliest possible date.

Mr. Speaker, I will be as brief as possible in order to facilitate quick passage of Bill C-150. However, I need to take a few moments because some of the things the Minister has said, as my hon. friend from Skeena has noted in side-long glances to me, have been, to say the least, provocative.
What the House is doing with Bill C-150 is once more amending the Indian Act. We are amending the Indian Act this time to correct a drafting error, or what the Minister called a "technical error", from a previous set of amendments to the same Act, a series of amendments presented by the Government in a Bill known as Bill C-31. That is a rather famous Bill among the Indian people of Canada. That Bill provided that persons who had lost their Indian status because of marriage or some other antiquated reason could now apply to have that status restored, and in some cases they could also have their membership in a band returned to them.
For a very long time in Canada the aspirations of governments was that somehow we do away with this special status that has been ascribed to Indian persons. We wanted to assimilate them and make them part of the nation in a way that ran counter to their own cultural aspirations, to their own view of themselves as nations who had entered into a treaty relationship with the Government of Canada. For at least 20 years that idea has been abandoned, although it keeps cropping up again. We are always nervous about this attempt to fail to recognize the special place that Indian people have in the Canadian nation.
In response to what the Minister said on Bill C-31, I want to say to the House that almost everything connected with Bill C-31 could be described as a litany of bungling. There has been goof-up after goof-up like a parade of clowns. First, the commitment from the Minister of the day, the predecessor to the current Minister, was that as a result of Bill C-31 "no band would be worse off'. Despite what the Minister said this morning, that commitment has not been lived up to. It has hardly been partially lived up to. There has been a monumental failure on the part of the Government to live up to its obligations under Bill C-31.
The costs that the Minister mentioned this morning that have gone to Indian people as a result of Bill C-31 have meant that there has been a curtailment in other areas. For example, the housing programs on Indian reserves have not been touched at all. The backlog has not been dented at all since 1984, not at all.
In addition, the Government has decided to put a cap on educational assistance for Indian young persons who are seeking entrance into universities and colleges. As of last September, because of the Government's action, 1,000 of these young people who qualified and had a place at a college or
university ready for them were denied access because the Government refused to fund them.
Despite pressure from the opposition Parties, an obligation in Bill C-31 for a parliamentary committee to review the impact of Bill C-31 was delayed and delayed and delayed. Now, Sir, at long last we have a report that is ready for the printer. However, why has that report not been presented to Parliament? It is because it is locked up in the chairman's office. Repeated telephone calls to the chairman's office have not brought any response at all. We do not even know where he is. Presumably he is out campaigning for re-election, which raises an interesting question: "Why would you want to seek re-election when you have not yet completed the job from the last time you were elected?"
When the legislative drafters put together Bill C-31 they erred in Clause 6(3) and Clause 11(3). Under those clauses it became possible in some cases to deny registration to an Indian person where an applicant's parents had died before April 17, 1985, or to deny band membership where an applicant's parents has died before June 28, 1987.
My friend, the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), in speaking at the committee stage, indicated to the House that that never ever was the intent. It was not the intent of the Government. It was not the intent of the committee which examined the Bill that that restriction should be there, but that is exactly what happened. In fact, the provisions of the Bill were to ensure that no applicant would be disadvantaged by parental death. That was the real purpose. It was meant to be inclusive and not to be exclusive. What went wrong?
What went wrong, Sir, was that someone in the Department of Justice-and one can only imagine what went on, whether the cribbage tournament had come to an end or all the crossword puzzles had been completed-picked up Bill C-31 and said: "Here is a way in which we can create a new obstacle to the registration of Indian persons". I am sure there must have been glee and jubilation in many of the burrows, hollows, and cubby-holes of the bureaucracy because a new obstacle had been discovered.
That always reminds me of the classic description of the difference between a bureaucrat and a public servant. A bureaucrat will always give a hundred reasons plus why something absolutely cannot be done, and a public servant will search diligently for a way to solve a problem and improve the life of a citizen.
However it happened, the death rule created an obstacle. Cooler heads realized that this had to be corrected. It was an injustice against Indian people. It was an interpretation of the Act that was never intended.
I want the House to know, both the government side and the opposition side, that there is a lesson here for all of us to learn. We should never, ever have blind faith or total trust in those who draft the Government's Bills. There is a tendency around here to think that anything that arrives out of the dens,
August 19, 1988

burrows, and hollows of the bureaucracy has to be letter perfect. There is a tendency to believe that. There is also a tendency to believe that parliamentarians are just a bunch of amateur lawmakers, and how could they ever conceivably correct something that has come out of the Department of Justice. Why, it is insulting and arrogant of parliamentarians to think that they could ever do that! Well, if that were so, I wonder why there are so many times in which we have to amend Bills in this House. It so often happens, Sir, because in many cases the law is in fact an ass. The law is an ass because it has been badly drafted. It has been drafted in a confusing way so that it creates enormous problems for some of our citizens or all of them, as the case may be.
We now have Bill C-150, and it is taking up important time of the House. Why? It is because there was careless drafting in the first place, and then, to add insult to injury, Justice decided to put its own twisted interpretation upon the drafting that it had done. It is causing a lot of difficulty for the House, but leave the House aside. I want you to know how much hurt has resulted from this for many Indian persons who have been seeking reinstatement, seeking to have their status restored, and have run up against this particular brick wall.
I thank you, Sir, and I thank the House for allowing me to get that grievance off my chest. I feel a little bit better for having done so. I want to say that we want this Bill to proceed quickly. My only concern is: Have we now got it right? My confidence obviously has been shaken. Have we now got it right, or will my hon. friend from Skeena and myself be told some time next year that as a result of Bill C-150 no one at all can apply to be reinstated, or of all those who have been reinstated, all those reinstatements are null and void? I know, Sir, that that is unlikely, and I am expressing my concerns in an extreme way. We have had our fingers burned here. I say to my friends in the House that we have to be cautious.
As a general rule, almost all Indian legislation that has been passed by this and successive Parliaments has been bad legislation, and most agreements that this Government and previous Governments have negotiated with Indian Nations have always been subject to those kinds of interpretations in which the Government of Canada comes out the winner and the Indian nation or the group of Indian nations that have involved themselves in that agreement have come out the losers. That is why Indian people have so much suspicion about the whole legislative process. That is why they pause and hesitate and delay when they sign agreements. They are always looking for that hook which will pull them down. They are always looking for the trick, for the con. There has been too much of that by Governments of the past.
Recently, a document came to my desk which contained a check list to be followed by those negotiators who wish to see issues resolved between the Government of Canada and Indian nations. There is no time for me to review that list and I do not intend to do it, but I want to make the point, briefly and
Indian Act
simply, that if Government-Indian relations in Canada are ever to improve, it is absolutely essential that we begin with a change in attitude, particularly on the part of those on the government side who are in face-to-face contact with Indian leaders, whether it is at the negotiating table or elsewhere. The so-called trust responsibility, which is so often referred to, has a variety of meanings and a variety of implications, but an elemental aspect of that is that we establish a climate of trust. Only in that climate can there be good and progressive and helpful work which can be done to improve Government-Indian relations.
I will conclude by saying that Bill C-150 has been examined-and the Minister mentioned this-by the Assembly of First Nations, by the Native Council of Canada, by my office, by our parliamentary counsel to the committee, and by my hon. friend from Skeena. It appears to be satisfactory, but, as that line goes in a play by G. B. Shaw by the very same title, "You never can tell, Sir. You never can tell".

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to put a few remarks on the record in relation to Bill C-150. As the Minister said, it is true that the Assembly of First Nations, the Native Council of Canada, and the Native Women's Association had a chance to look at the draft of this Bill, but not because of anything the Government had done. I sent a copy of the draft over to them on Monday so that they would have an opportunity to have a look at it before it came before the House this morning.
It is true, as my friend from Cochrane-Superior and the Minister have said, that it appears to meet the test of allowing those who have been denied the opportunity to be reinstated to have that done now. I was pleased to hear the Minister say that it is fully retroactive to April 17, 1985. Those who are now allowed to have their registration process go forward here in Ottawa will have all those benefits and entitlements that they have been denied these past three years given to them in one lump, once they are registered and have their status returned.
The registration entitlement was first consolidated in the Indian Act in 1876, and here we stand, 112 years later, adding one more chip to the pile of problems and complex rules that are very, very technical. My friend from Cochrane-Superior and I, heard evidence on Bill C-31 for many months, beginning last September until June, indicating that there are probably very few, perhaps only a handful, of Canadians who actually understand all the highly technical and complex rules that apply to women and to those who have different blood quantum, those second generations rules and all those things the Government of Canada has seen fit to bring in over the last 112 years.
I hope that this is a stepping stone, that Parliament will soon listen to what the First Nations have been saying and give serious and determined consideration to the concept of selfgovernment and self-determination, so that it is the First Nations that decide citizenship, status, and band membership,

August 19, 1988
Indian Act
rather than Parliament continuing to bring forward ever more complex, highly technical, legal language.
Those applying for reinstatement or first time registration face an unbelievable bureaucratic nightmare, as we have heard from the witnesses who came before our standing committee in relation to Bill C-31. Everyone recognizes that the death rule that we are amending today is a legal defect, that it was not the intention of this House or of any Party to bring it forward. As my friend from Cochrane-Superior stated so well, there is a distinct difference between bureaucrats and public servants and between interpretation by the Department of Justice and the interests of those who want to see Parliament act. First, Clause 6(3) results in a denial of registration for an applicant whose parents died before April 17, 1985, or, second, Clause 11(3) results in a denial of band membership for an applicant whose parents died before June 28, 1987.
We must keep in mind that these amendments came into force in 1985 in order to ensure compliance with international human rights standards and the equality provisions of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, to a great extent thanks to the work of Miss Lovelace who took this matter all the way to the United Nations. Bill C-31 did not come in of its own volition. It was only under international pressure that Canada brought it into compliance with international human rights standards.
The Government originally estimated 65,000 applicants for reinstatement between 1985 and 1990. Now, 118,000 are expected, according to government estimates, and we have heard evidence before the committee that it may run far higher than that, up to 130,000 or more.
We do not know how many individuals are blocked by the death rule, but we do know that the Minister and the Government have known for more than a year and have done nothing. Bill C-150 should have been before this House a year ago. Applications have been simply held in limbo, kept on ice across the river in Hull.
By May of 1988, over 100,000 applications had come in. Some 54 per cent were from adults and some 46 per cent were from minors. Likely hundreds are held up by the death rule because only 52 per cent of the over 100,000 applications have been completed by the Government. Some 74 per cent of completions have resulted in new registrations with 26 per cent disallowance. The applications by region were the highest from Ontario with 29,000. British Columbia was second with 18,000 and Alberta was third with 13,000; then came Manitoba with
12.000,	Quebec with 11,000, Saskatchewan with 10,000, the Atlantic region with 4,000, the Northwest Territories with
2.000,	and Yukon with 2,500.
Registration delay has had far-reaching impacts on thousands of individuals in terms of health care, education, housing, residents taxation, and, in particular, participation in culture and membership in their home communities and
nations. This amendment has been a long time in coming, and it is shameful that once again the First Nations are treated to such second-class treatment by any Government.
I want to touch briefly on a comment made by my friend, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). He quoted David Crombie when he was the Minister responsible who said: "No band would be worse off'. We have heard evidence from across the country, including both Yukon and the N.W.T., and we have been unable to find a band of the close to 600 bands in Canada that is not worse off. It is a tragedy that a promise in relation to something which came about because of the good work of the United Nations could not be lived up to by a Government of Canada.
I want to conclude by referring to the Bill C-31 report of the standing committee which relates directly to the death rules. We have the draft, as my hon. friend pointed out, and it has been locked up in the chairman's office for two months now. The Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior, myself, and two members from the government side have now taken the extraordinary measure of invoking Standing Order 92(2) of this Chamber to order the chairman to come back to Ottawa to do what he is paid to do. Beyond his pay as a Member of Parliament, he is paid to chair the committee.
I have been trying to get a return call for a long time, as I know has my friend from Cochrane-Superior. I would hope that the chairman of the committee would find some way, either with a road-map, on an aircraft, or some other way, to get back to Ottawa and make the report which is required by statute.
As of June, 1987, our standing committee was required to report to Parliament forthwith under a statutory requirement. How many Canadians have been dragged before the courts for not living up to a law? Here we have a standing committee with seven Members of Parliament including five government Members, one Liberal Member, and one New Democrat, who have been unable, in 14 months, to live up to a statutory requirement to report forthwith on the impact of Bill C-31 on the First Nations of Canada.
I would hope that as a result of this debate, and perhaps with the assistance of the Minister who is here today, a call might be made to the chairman of that committee to return to Ottawa. If he does not comply, he will be dragged here pursuant to Standing Order 92(2), being in flagrant violation of the wishes of the standing committee, to report on Bill C-31 which has extensive technical information on the death rules and on the over-all impact of Bill C-31 on the First Nations.
In the interests of the more than one million first citizens of Canada and members of the First Nations, I would hope that the Minister would take just such action today to ensure that the Member from Cape Breton returns to Ottawa and does what he should with regard to the death rules and Bill C-31, that is, report on that Bill to Parliament and the people of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point or order. I think you would find a predisposition in the Chamber to attempt, in relatively expeditious fashion, to finish report stage of this Bill and then to go immediately to third reading stage.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point or order. We agree that Bill C-123 can be dealt with expeditiously. Speaking for this Party, it is not even necessary for there to be any speeches at the third reading stage. The Bill was extensively debated at second reading and has been before the committee.
I will be satisfied if I have at least the opportunity to submit for consideration one of two amendments. I understand that my first amendment was ruled out of order, and I understand that the second one has been ruled in order. If there can be consideration by the House of this amendment and an explanation by myself about why I introduced it, that will suffice and I think we could conclude consideration of this Bill very quickly.

Mr. Speaker, on the same point of order, I would like just a few moments to put some remarks on the record in relation to Bill C-123. It does involve trust accounts that are being held in the Consolidated Revenue Fund of Canada involving over $900 million. I think it is important that some concluding remarks in relation to Bill C-123 be put on the record.

I assume that those remarks would be put at third reading. I have a ruling by the Speaker with respect to Bill C-123, an Act to amend the Indian Act (minors' funds and surviving spouse's preferential share).
There are two motions in amendment set down on the Notice Paper in relation to Bill C-123. Motion No. 1 causes the Chair some difficulty because it seeks to amend the original Act, contrary to Citation 773(8) of Beauchesne's Fifth Edition which reads as follows:
(8)(a) An amendment may not amend a statute which is not before the committee. Journals, March 28, 1969, p. 862. Journals, June 11, 1970, p. 993.
(b) An amendment may not amend sections from the original Act unless they are specifically being amended in a clause of the bill before the committee. Debates, December 15, 1977, p. 1909.
Therefore, I must rule that Motion No. 1 is out of order, as the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior indicated.
Motion No. 2 is in order and I will now put Motion No. 2 to the House.

Motion No. 2
That Bill C-123 be amended in Clause 3 by striking out lines 13 to 15 at page 3 and substituting the following therefor:
"and who the council determined to be the parent or person to whom the payment is to be made or, if so requested by the council on giving its consent to that distribution, to the council to be held in trust and paid for the maintenance, advancement or other benefit of the child to a parent or person who is responsible for the care and custody of the child and who the council determines to be the parent or person to whom the payment is to be made."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this amendment moves to delete certain lines in Bill C-123 and replace them with the motion before you. The purpose of this is simple, that is, to provide for the exclusion of provincial social services in the distribution of minors' trust funds.
My hon. friends in the House ought to be aware that there is a very deep and abiding resentment on the part of Indian nations toward direct interference by a provincial jurisdiction in their affairs. At every opportunity they attempt to make it clear that their relationship is a special relationship with the Government of Canada, a relationship underscored by treaties which have been entered into and by the fact of our Constitution itself, namely, Section 91(24) which says that Indians and lands reserved for Indians are an exclusive federal responsibility-
This amendment simply says that minors' trust funds which now go to parents, guardians of Indian children, or band councils, may not be grabbed by provincial agencies. That is the purpose, Sir, and I would like the House to give serious consideration to that motion to improve Bill C-123.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think I should tell the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) that while we now have to move on to Statements by Members and Question Period, if the Hon. Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has peculiar ideas on the environment and the economy. Its priority actually seems to be

August 19, 1988
pollution. Look, for example, at the way in which the Western Diversification Fund is spent.
From a memo released by the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) summarizing projects funded so far, we learn that Vicell Canada Tissue Limited in Delta, British Columbia, receives $4.6 million of taxpayers' money "to manufacture dry formed tissue for sale to paper converters who will produce end products such as wipes, disposable towelling, and serviettes". From the same memo we learn that ISCA Management of Vancouver gets $21,000 "to market a proposal to the U.S. Department of Energy for a $1-million research and development project on acid rain control systems".
What a strange sense of priorities for this Government, spending 200 times more on the production of more litter than on the prevention of acid rain. Would you not agree, Mr. Speaker?

Mr. Speaker, on August 20, 1968, Czechoslovakia's hopes for freedom and independence were crushed when Soviet troops invaded the city of Prague. The invaders came to crush the Prague Spring, a brave experiment in independence. Soviet troops occupy Czechoslovakia to this day.
Canada was the beneficiary of this sad episode. Thousands of Czechs and Slovaks emigrated here and have since made enormous contributions to their new home. Let us not forget the terrible price that the people of Czechoslovakia paid for the attempts to reform their society.
Today, when so many of the rights and freedoms Canadians enjoy are denied to the Czechoslovakian people by a Soviet puppet regime, let us join together with Czechoslovakians in commemorating the twentieth anniversary of their brave attempt to restore freedom and justice in Czechoslovakia.

Mr. Speaker, Hamilton has one more example of the disastrous corporate plans that are so characteristic of Canada Post. Not only is this government corporation jeopardizing Canadian jobs and cutting back essential services, it is also potentially responsible
for the demolition of an historical building in downtown Hamilton.
Canada Post announced plans earlier this month for a new postal plant to replace the present antiquated facilities. It plans to do this by demolishing a building of historical importance. The local architectural conservation advisory committee cannot give the building historical designation without Canada Post's approval. This just shows how little this corporation cares about the communities it serves.
There is unfortunately little hope that Canada Post will listen to the concerns of Hamiltonians. After all, it has not cared about the women and men who have lost a decent living wage because of privatization. It has not listened to the citizens of rural Canada who have fewer and fewer postal services, and it certainly has not listened to the seniors and the disabled people who no longer get door-to-door service.

subtopic: NATIONAL POLICY-CREATION OF JOBS BY SMALL BUSINESSES
NATIONAL POLICY-CREATION OF JOBS BY SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, "as a nation we rely upon the ability of Canadian entrepreneurs to identify new business opportunities, to respond to them, and to convert a creative idea into a prosperous business".
These were the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney) in introducing the new national policy on entrepreneurship on August 16, just three days ago. Of the 1.25 million new jobs created since 1984, 80 per cent have been in the small business sector. This only goes to prove that in Canada, small business is big business.
The new national policy will create the right climate so that Canadian entrepreneurs can be even more successful in the future.

Mr. Speaker, when will Conservatives realize that Hamilton is not just the receptacle of the country's garbage? The Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock) actually accused Hamilton of "holding the country to ransom" yesterday.
Meanwhile, where are the Conservative Members from Hamilton? I have not heard the Hon. Member for Hamilton West (Mr. Peterson), the Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin), the Hon. Member for Burlington (Mr. Kempling) or the Hon. Member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott) speak out to defend Hamilton. Why elect Conservatives in the
August 19, 1988

city of Hamilton when they will not defend the interests of the people of Hamilton when the federal Government tries to use us as a receptacle for their garbage?
The odyssey of the garbage is not over. They are now planning to send it off to Gatineau. I guess Quebec is good enough for their garbage. What is good enough for Hamilton and Gatineau is not good enough for the city of Toronto or the garbage facilities at the airport.
The federal Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) is responsible. He created this situation and he should resolve it. The Hamilton Members should speak up for Hamilton.

Mr. Speaker, recently the Government received a long-awaited report entitled "Energy and Canadians into the 21st Century". This is the first thorough review of national energy policy in 30 years.
The report indicates that by virtually any measure one might wish to apply, Canada is rich in energy. However, energy wealth does not guarantee a secure future. The luxury of having options carries the need to make difficult choices.
The report recommends that Canada's energy should be used to its economic potential, that environmental goals should have the same importance as economic and social goals, that energy resources should be developed because of market mechanisms, and that commitment to research, development and management of technology is critical to enhancing Canada's energy choices and environmental quality into the next century.
The report paints a future that is challenging and optimistic. It also concludes that Canadians will receive substantive national economic and regional development opportunities through enhanced energy trade. Furthermore, the report concludes that the proportional access clause in the trade agreement can be implemented in a way which does not prejudice Canada's energy security interests.

Mr. Speaker, once again the Port of Churchill's fate is before the federal Government. Rarely has a shipping season gone by when Manitobans have not had a fight on their hands to see that the port remains alive as a shipping centre and a vital part of our nation's sea port system. This year is no exception.
My letter to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in June calling for a full commitment to the port has yet to be answered, even though it was written some two months ago. Almost one month ago the Prime Minister gave Manitoba's Premier a commitment that he would personally look into the matter of the Port of Churchill and provide action. What is the Prime Minister waiting for? Even his promises of fast action to the Premier of Manitoba seem to be meaningless.
Manitobans want fairness. The Port of Churchill is crucial for farmers in its catchment area, and it represents substantial savings for those who use it. The potential for a longer season grows as the port is used, not only for the products of other western producers but for other products such as lumber from Manfor in The Pas.
It is a shame that politics is ruining Churchill. The one thing that is required to keep Churchill's potential alive is political will, and I call upon the Prime Minister to keep his promises to the people of Churchill.

maintopic: CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
CANADA-UNITED STATES FREE TRADE AGREEMENT-POSITION OF LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, while speaking to a group of people in my riding, the Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) made some erroneous statements regarding the free trade agreement with the United States. The fact is that he failed to tell the people that Canadian control of unprocessed fish is fully protected by the binational dispute settlement process. He failed to tell the people that the tariff elimination for crab products over 10 years will allow Canadian crab processors to remain price competitive in the U.S. market should the significant Alaska crab fishery become a factor in the U.S. market.
We respect the Hon. Member's right to be opposed to free trade, but we also expect him to have the decency to tell the people the truth.

Mr. Speaker, there is disappointment for Canadian families with the proposed, poorly conceived Tory child care plan. It fails to understand that adequate child care is not a luxury, it is a necessity.
Canadians now know all too well the market driven Tory philosophy that promotes profits first and policy charades next,

August 19, 1988
For what you see is not what you get. The old shell game is how they play the policy game. While the Tory plan talks about 200,000 spaces, it forgets the need for fully accessible and affordable child care for one million Canadian children awaiting spaces.
[DOT] (mo)
How can Tories defend their child care plan? It says nothing about lower or middle income families being helped. It forgets latchkey children. It makes less spaces available, compared to the old plan. It fails to ensure quality standards across all provinces. It is silent on workplace standards, workplace child care, and extending parental leave. It is a closed program.
What happens after seven years? The Conservatives expect Canadians to be pleased about the increased child care expense deduction. It gives a larger tax break to the well-to-do while costing millions to the Treasury. It does nothing for lower income families who cannot afford to pay taxes.
This tax break is no help to those who need it. Tax credits would have been a fairer way. Canadians will not forgive the Tories for their four-year, too poor, too short plan for children. Liberals consider child care a basic building block.

subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT OF MONTREAL SOUTH SHORE

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean-Guy Hudon (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT OF MONTREAL SOUTH SHORE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on July 14, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Bouchard) gave a very important press conference in Beauharnois. In front of more than more than 400 people, he announced that the federal Government, in particular the Department of Transport, would take part in the regional development of the South Shore of Montreal, called "Monteregie" in French.
The federal Government made it clear that Highway 30, like other expressways, is a provincial responsibility, but that since this highway crosses federal property, the federal Government will connect the two shores with no mechanical hindrance. This commitment from the Minister is worth nearly $100 million.
This positive initiative has been demanded for 25 years and the South Shore of Montreal is very proud of this announcement. The mayors have understood that it is the result of the cooperation of the South Shore mayors with their provincial MNAs and federal MPs, the leadership of the Beauharnois-Salaberry Regional Municipality at the Monteregie Summit and of the Committee to Complete Highway 30 chaired by Beauharnois Mayor Claude Haineault.
At last, Sorel will be connected to Valleyfield and to Highway 20, which passes it, via the Trans-Canada Highway, the Eastern Townships Autoroute and the highway to Saint-Jean.
On the eve of the election, there is much talk about election promises. We are accused of merely making election promises. As far as I know, Mr. Speaker, we are not in an election campaign; this is a commitment by the Minister and it is worth at least as much as the written promise or letter that the Leader of the Opposition is supposed to make public during the election campaign for the same thing. This is only an election promise while ours is a commitment.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure you are aware that yesterday the Bank of Canada increased interest rates to some 9.8 per cent. In Saskatoon, all the Premiers condemned the Government's high interest policy, including the Premier of Ontario, the province that has benefited most from economic growth in the last year.
In addition, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has condemned the high interest rate policy of the Government, saying that it is hurting the farmers of the country. In addition, the National Farmers Union has condemned this high interest policy. As well, Roger Phillips, President of IPSCO, has made the same kind of statement.
On behalf of Canadians, particularly farmers from western Canada, I want to plead with the Government to come to its senses and bring down interest rates before it throws a lot of people out of work and hurts exporters, hurts western Canadian farmers, and indeed farmers across the country.

Mr. Speaker, almost four years have passed since the Government came to office. During those four years many very exciting things have happened. We have the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. During each of those four years we had the greatest economic growth of any country in the world. We had the greatest job creation of any country in the world.
On top of that, we have the first ever agreement with respect to reducing acid rain emissions in this country. We have the
August 19, 1988

first ever employment equity legislation. Now before Parliament we have the first ever national child care legislation.
Many of my constituents believe that the child care program is the most important thing Parliament has dealt with and should be dealing with. In fact, contrary to the assertion by the Member for Mount Royal (Mrs. Finestone), many of my constituents are telling me not to hold an election until we have passed that child care legislation.

subtopic: GARBAGE PAIL KIDS CARDS-BAN ON IMPORTATION URGED
GARBAGE PAIL KIDS CARDS-BAN ON IMPORTATION URGED
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I brought to the attention of Parliament that obscene bubble gum cards were being sold to the children of Canada. These are known as Garbage Pail Kids cards. As I indicated previously, they depict babies and small children in the form of dolls being mutilated.
The American company involved, trying to justify this grotesque sale of products to children, is reported as saying to the Canadian Press:
''Kids have always liked gross", said Norman Liss of The Topps Company.
''And this is a gross product."
Mr. Liss is certainly correct in his last statement. This is a gross product. To be selling us this kind of garbage is a gross abuse of their privilege of being able to sell in this country.
Again I call upon the Government to utilize the provisions of Section 159 and Section 160 of the Criminal Code of Canada to stop the importation and sale of these kinds of products. For my part, I have referred the matter to the Crown Attorney here in Ottawa and have asked him to look at the situation with a view to laying charges, so that our children are not polluted by this kind of nonsense.

subtopic: CALL FOR PASSAGE OF FREE TRADE LEGISLATION
CALL FOR PASSAGE OF FREE TRADE LEGISLATION

That is an insult to all Canadians. That request is a desperate act by a desperate man seeking publicity. It is harmful to western Canada and all Canadians.
Oral Questions
I call on the Upper House to carry out its responsibility, exercise its independent judgment and pass the Bill, until such time as we are able to reform the Senate and have an elected Senate rather than a bunch of unelected people from the Liberal Party.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subsubtopic: PATRONAGE ALLEGATIONS ATTRIBUTED TO FORMER MINISTER-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY RCMP
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister and concerns a very serious matter.
For the first time, a Conservative Member of Parliament, a member of the Privy Council and former member of the Prime Minister's Cabinet, has stated that the Conservative Government is involved in a kickback scheme.
The Conservative Member acuses the Conservative Government of routinely resorting to a system that according to her, violates the Criminal Code of Canada.
Yesterday in the House, the Deputy Prime Minister stated that his colleague's statements were, to use his own words, half-truths, falsehoods, innuendo, distortions of facts and smear.
How can the Deputy Prime Minister make such a statement? Was there an investigation by the RCMP? The Deputy Commissioner said there was none.
In the circumstances, will the Deputy Prime Minister ensure that the RCMP will conduct an investigation to clarify the statements made by Conservative Member for Rosemont?

subsubtopic: PATRONAGE ALLEGATIONS ATTRIBUTED TO FORMER MINISTER-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION BY RCMP

Mr. Speaker, I can advise the House that we as a Government have no information whatsoever to substantiate the allegations made by the Hon. Member for Rosemont. I am also advised by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that at no time has the Hon. Member for Rosemont ever spoken to the RCMP with respect to those allegations.
Notwithstanding that, I can advise the Right Hon. Member that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police will be interviewing the Member for Rosemont with respect to those allegations.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. On February 3 of this year the Prime Minister said, and I use the Prime Minister's words: "The integrity of this Government

August 19, 1988
Oral Questions
and all its members is the responsibility of the Prime Minister".
Yesterday when the Prime Minister was in Waterloo, Ontario, when he was asked about the statement made about criminal activity by his own Member of Parliament for Rosemont-whom the Prime Minister once had in his Cabinet-the Prime Minister said: "I have no idea. What do you think?" That flippant remark by a Prime Minister is a dereliction of duty in the face of an allegation, a statement made by one of his own Members, relating to criminal activity.
This does not come from our side of the House. This comes from one of the Prime Minister's own Members. What is the Prime Minister actively going to do to deal with this situation in accordance with his statement made in this House on February 3?

Mr. Speaker, I think the right hon. gentleman would agree that the Government of Canada, under the leadership of the Prime Minister, has moved very quickly with respect to various charges of wrongdoing, such as the establishment of the Commission of Inquiry, ministerial dismissal, and investigations, and where there has been clear evidence that there might be wrongdoing or contraventions of the Criminal Code, immediate action was taken.
What we have here is a broad statement which is not substantiated-and I think the Hon. Member for Rosemont referred to that-vague charges which really cast an unfortunate shadow upon all elected Members of this House and that, I submit, does very little to enhance the integrity of public office holders.
I would also ask the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition what he intends to do with his justice critic who yesterday made a statement, and I will quote from this morning's Ottawa Citizen:
Jensen confirmed that the FBI had asked the RCMP for assistance in investigating whether payments had been made by an American corporation to Canadian politicians or Conservative Party officials considered to be lobbyists but not registered as such as required by U.S. law.
I am advised by the Assistant Commissioner, through the Solicitor General, that at no time did he ever state, confirm or imply that the FBI had asked the RCMP for assistance as stated by the Hon. Member. What we have here is this Member attempting to use the RCMP for political partisan gain, and it is a tactic I abhor and one which all members of this House should abhor. He should have the decency and fortitude to stand up and apologize and withdraw.
Hear, hear!
I will get up at twelve o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I intend to deal with that in just a second. Just for the moment I will conclude the exchange I had with the Hon. Solicitor General and the Deputy Prime Minister on the statements made by the
Conservative Member for Rosemont. I suggest that an interview by the RCMP with the Member is not sufficient. They should follow the Member's own suggestion and have a Royal Commission to investigate the whole course of conduct of the Government.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister as well. It concerns the issue that won't go away. The Member for Rosemont is quoted in today's Toronto Star as saying:
Look, there are people who told me at a certain time they were aware that when you receive a government contract from Ottawa, you have to return a certain amount to the kitty.
Did the Deputy Prime Minister ask the Member of Parliament for Rosemont how she found out about these alleged kickbacks? If he has not done so yet, when does he intend to do so? And has the Prime Minister contacted the Member for Rosemont? It has been two days now since the Government has known about this.

Considering the fact that public morality rests on his shoulders, I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister when he contacted the Hon. Member for Rosemont, and if he has not done so, will he do so today? And if not, why not? After all, it's his responsibility!

Indian Act

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-123, an Act to amend the Indian Act (minors' funds and surviving spouse's preferential share), as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee; and on the amendment of Mr. Penner (p. 18559).

Mr. Speaker, when we moved to Question Period I was in the midst of explaining to the House why an amendment which I have proposed to Bill C-123 should merit the consideration of the House and inclusion into this statute.
I want to explain to the Minister that this particular amendment, which has behind it the consent, authority, and wishes of the Indian Association of Alberta, was not introduced before the legislative committee at the appropriate time simply because there had been a communications gap; that is to say, legal counsel for the Indian Association of Alberta, Mr. Mandamin, had indicated in his appearance before the committee that he had such an amendment and felt that it was an amendment that was in keeping with the intent of the statute but would deal with one flaw that they regarded as being serious.
On the day the amendment was to be received, the committee delayed its proceedings, hoping to receive it by fax, but as a result of a misunderstanding about when the committee was to sit that particular day, we never did receive the amendment. However, I made a commitment to Mr. Mandamin that I would introduce this amendment at report stage.
Therefore, I want the House to know that this is not a matter that has been dealt with at the committee stage. It was part of the brief presented by the Vice-Chief of the Assembly of First Nations who represents the Province of Alberta.
The purpose of the amendment is to exclude any right of provincial authorities to the trust moneys that are now going to be under the authority of the band or of the parents or guardians, up to the limit of $3,000 or more if that is agreed to by Order in Council.
The Indian Association of Alberta takes the position that the authority of the province into matters of First Nations is an unwarranted authority. I believe that when they make that assertion they are on very sound constitutional ground.
I believe the Government of Canada would probably lean in the direction of that kind of interpretation. I do not need to quote to the House Section 91(24), the first part of our Constitution under the British North America Act. Certainly that federal authority was reasserted again in Section 35 of the most recent changes to the Canadian Constitution.
August 19, 1988
There is clearly a federal authority and clearly a relationship between the Government of Canada and the First Nations. In other words, the relationship that was described in treaties is a relationship between the First Nations and the Crown. The interpretation is that the Crown is resident in the Government of Canada and has not been distributed widely across the country, so there are Crown rights giving authority to provinces or territorial Governments over Indian people.
That is exactly the rationale for establishing what we call Indian child welfare agencies. This has been done in the Province of Manitoba. Quite properly, the Indian leaders in Manitoba recognized at the outset that in establishing child welfare agencies it was very advisable to receive as much expertise as they could from the provincial authorities because child welfare as such is not an area that belongs to the federal Government. Therefore, we do not have the depository of expertise.
In the Province of Manitoba, a tripartite agreement was the first step toward establishing a child welfare agency. That was done more than five years ago by an agreement that was negotiated between Canada, Manitoba, and the Indian leaders in that province.
During the five to six year period that has intervened up to the present, a body of expertise has developed in Manitoba for child welfare agencies. They are now seeking a new bilateral agreement, with the transfer of funds, so that they can entirely take over this responsibility.
There has been a problem. This new agreement has not been reached. The Government of Canada is delaying. There are a number of difficulties. I will leave it to the Minister who was present in the House today to explain exactly why that is happening. However, I do not want to make that the point of my argument.
The point of my argument is that we are moving in the direction of establishing child welfare agencies for Indian people. The reason for that is that Indian leaders find it abhorrent that provincial agencies, using provincial Child Care Acts, should move in under the provisions of those Acts, take children out of Indian homes, and place them in non-Indian foster homes. In some cases they were adopted by non-Indian people. These youngsters, therefore, lost their culture, tradition, background, and heritage. In fact, there were a great many cases where these children were not only adopted into non-Indian homes but were adopted right out of the country altogether. They were adopted into American homes and only discovered many years later, in some cases, that in fact they came from Canada and that their heritage and ancestry was Indian. This caused enormous distress, psychological, spiritual, and personal. That is why we are moving away from that kind of situation. The Government is sympathetic and accepts that premise, but we are just moving much too slowly.
August 19, 1988

That is the background for the amendment. The amendments I am proposing to the House will simply say that in transferring to bands the authority over minor trust funds, the band wants to be in the position of saying with authority who can have access to those funds. Of course, the statute with which we are dealing says that authority can be with the parent or with the guardian. The statute is of particular interest in the Province of Alberta where there are large amounts of money in the trust funds because of the oil and gas revenue. Mr. Mandamin, legal counsel for the Indian Association of Alberta, argues that where a child is taken into custody by provincial authorities, that custodian should not have the authority to cease the trust funds. The amendment I am proposing will simple make it clear in law that it cannot be done.
I want to repeat again that we have to understand in approving this amendment that the provincial authority, vis-avis Indian people, is at best ambiguous and uncertain. It is an area in which we still have a great deal of work to do. It is part of what those First Ministers' conferences were about, to try to define and clarify aboriginal rights, to describe with some degree of accuracy what is the status of Indian people within Canada. This still remains an uncertain area, an area in which academics and learned legal counsel become involved, but we cannot leave it to those people. It is in the political arena, the realm of politics, that we can solve this problem. We can solve it at the negotiating table.
We cannot bite off all that today when dealing with Bill C-123. I ask the forgiveness of the Minister in reaching rather far with a matter that will have to be faced some day. Meanwhile, here is a small gesture, a small movement in the right direction.
1 understand the Government's opposition to the amendment because it has already looked at it. I have a memo from the special assistant to the Minister in charge of legislation. The argument is one that I simply cannot accept. The argument, very briefly stated, is that it is imperative that Indian children be treated in a manner consistent with the law affecting all other children in Canada. That is precisely the point. The Indian leaders are saying that their status is a special status, confirmed now in the Constitution. They have a relationship to Canada. Therefore, this equality of treatment which would involve a provincial jurisdiction on First Nations is not acceptable.
Therefore, I ask the Minister to take a look at the amendment. Unless he finds it exceedingly offensive in some other way I have failed to take due note of, I ask, speaking on behalf of the Indian Association of Alberta and its legal counsel, him to give serious consideration to incorporating this modest amendment into Bill C-123. It would still not make the Bill entirely and completely satisfactory to the Assembly of First Nations or to the Indian Association of Alberta because there are a few other flaws, that I will mention at third reading.
Indian Act
However, by and large we accept the Bill. It moves in the right direction. We are not in any way raising obstacles to the Bill. Here is one gesture, one movement, which will go a long way in recognizing what ought to be done in Canada; that is to say, First Nations have a particular kind of relationship with Canada and that has been gone into at great length in other forums. Certainly, it is demonstrated in no other way better than by the fact that these people have treaties with the Crown in the name of the Government of Canada. That is not a claim that can be made by any other group of Canadians of which I am aware.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak briefly to the motion presently before the House. I think the Minister has to give it very serious consideration. Frankly, I can think of no reason why in good faith the Minister would not agree to have this amendment brought forward.
To give a bit of coverage as to what has happened to date, I think it is necessary to expand on the remarks of my friend, the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). As the Minister will know, on July 28, the legislative committee hurried that morning to go through Bill C-123 while we were waiting for Mr. Mandamin's amendments to arrive. They were coming from Alberta to the AFN offices, and then they were going to be brought by some kind of messenger service to the committee. Through a series of unfortunate delays, they did not actually get to the committee. If the Minister or any member of this House would like to review the public record of the legislative committee, they will find that while we were examining Bill C-123, members who were there from all three Parties gave a commitment to look at Mr. Mandamin's amendments as soon as we could obtain them. We were going to get together and do that. I know the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior and I and our offices have attempted to get government Members who were on the legislative committee at that time together right up until today, and that has not been possible.
We promised on the record in the absence of Mr. Mandamin, who appeared as witness with the Vice-Chief of the Assembly of First Nations on this very important Bill, that we would look at those proposed amendments. The Speaker has already ruled out the first amendment since it touches on another piece of legislation, but I think there is a responsibility of the Minister to accept this proposed amendment. If he looks carefully at the words to be added, he will see that is a very small part of self-government. It is a very small part of determining the future of many children.
My friend touched upon the severe problem that has plagued aboriginal people in Canada for more than a century, and there have been the more recent developments of provincial apprehension laws. We know that not just hundreds and thousands but tens of thousands of the children of first citizen have been apprehended. I know from personal knowledge, having been a probation officer, that in many cases they have been apprehended on the flimsiest of grounds and not just put

August 19, 1988
Indian Act
into another home or adopted but, as my friend pointed out, many have been taken into the United States and elsewhere.
We encourage the Minister to look very carefully at the wording of the amendment wherein it states:
"and who the council determined to be the parent or person to whom the payment is to be made"-
That refers directly in most situations to the superintendent of child welfare in most of the provinces or territories. The amendment goes on to state:
"-to be held in trust and paid for the maintenance, advancement or other benefit of the child to a parent or person who is responsible for the care and custody of the child and who the council determines to be the parent or person to whom the payment is to be made."
What that does is very clear, and I think the Minister should understand it. It is an attempt to provide back to the council some greater potential for protection and for the benefit and future of the child. I think the Government would be remiss in terms of the promise of the legislative committee to deal with this in report stage. We are doing now what the committee proposed could and should be done. I think it is very important that this proposal be in the legislation because just as Mr. Goodwin, who appeared before the committee pointed out, there is extensive study being done within the Department on how to provide for mechanisms to return a large amount of funds.
I remind the Minister that in terms of minors' trusts there is over $135 million, and in terms of estates and minors' trusts combined there is over $900 million presently under the control of the Minister of Indian Affairs and the Minister of Finance. Surely, if we are moving toward what I think Mr. Goodwin in good faith said the Government was doing, which is returning complete jurisdiction and control of those type of trust accounts to first nations, then it is extremely important.
Let us be frank with respect to how long it has taken this Bill to get here. It required investigations two years in a row by the Auditor General. It required all kinds of other investigation. In fact, we know from officials of the Department that there has been widespread lawbreaking going on in the Department in relation to minors' trusts and to estates for many years.
I think this small step at least in terms of children in relation to the bands and the parents having more direct guardianship control and trust control of those funds is what Mr. Mandamin is suggesting. He has canvassed the working group. I confirmed that with him again yesterday. This is a very important amendment for more than just the moment 20,000 children who are directly affected at the present moment.
I urge the Minister to be flexible and to agree, as I do for my Party and I know the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior does for his Party, to have this rather small but important protective amendment included in Bill C-123.

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism) and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened with attention to the comments made by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) and the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton). I want them to know that we have looked carefully at the proposed amendment.
As I was listening to the Hon. Member for Cochrane- Superior talk about child welfare and explain in a few words how difficult it was, how big an issue it was and how much more work was required to be done, he said, and I quote: "We can't buy that off in this Bill"; that is to say, resolving the whole question of aboriginal rights and constitutional protection of those rights and recognition as to what they are.
The Hon. Member for Skeena says that this amendment would be a gesture of good will, a first element of selfgovernment. I have a great deal of sympathy for that argument because I believe that aboriginal Canadians should have the right of self-government. However, if we accept this amendment today, without these other issues being resolved, it will mean that we allow a band council at its discretion to refuse to make the payment of moneys belonging to a minor. That is what we would do. Until these other important questions are settled, I do not think it would be prudent to give that power to the band council to achieve this other objective with which I have sympathy. Then we would allow a band council the power to refuse the payment of money to a minor or to the person who is in fact responsible for that minor. That is what could happen.
For that reason and that reason alone-and it is a good enough reason because I believe that an independent child is entitled to expect that money to be paid to the person who is responsible for his care and custody-I do not think that this Indian child should be prevented from getting payment because the band council would prefer it or does not like the fact that the person actually having care and custody is not a person of their liking.
For that very good reason we cannot accept the amendment. We have given it serious consideration.
